extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying category theory and module theory
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-notes style exposition about direct limits (filtered colimits), their properties, tensor products of modules, and the beginnings of flatness theory, including universal properties, exactness results, and key examples/counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left adjoints preserve direct limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Every left adjoint F : C -> C' preserves direct limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (6.12). Proof reduces existence of unique induced map via adjunction and the universal mapping property (UMP) of the direct limit. Use the adjoint equivalence to translate diagrams into ones where the UMP of the limit applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functor categories inherit direct limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If C has direct limits indexed by a small category J, then the functor category C^I (functors I -> C) also has direct limits indexed by J.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition (6.13). Construct the limit object pointwise: for fixed object of I, take the limit over J of the corresponding evaluation functors; check compatibility and the UMP. The proof shows how natural transformations induced by arrows in I produce compatible squares (6.13.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct limits commute (interchange of colimits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given categories I and J and a functor M : J -> C^I (equivalently a bifunctor J x I -> C), the colimit over J of the colimit over I equals the colimit over I of the colimit over J: lim_J lim_I M = lim_I lim_J M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (6.14). Uses that evaluation functors are left adjoints (6.6) and previous results (6.12, 6.13). Useful when computing iterated colimits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct limit functor preserves coproducts and coequalizers (in Sets and R-mod)
rubrics_metrics.description: For I a small category, lim_I : C^I -> C preserves coproducts and coequalizers when C is Sets or R-mod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary (6.15). This is because coproducts and coequalizers are special cases of direct limits and C has them; then (6.14) implies preservation. Use when exchanging finite/colimit constructions with formation of limits over diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of filtered category
rubrics_metrics.description: A small category I is filtered if: (1) for any objects i and j there exists k and maps i -> k and j -> k; (2) for any parallel morphisms f,g : i => j there exists k and φ : j -> k with φ∘f = φ∘g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition (7.1). Filtered categories generalize directed posets; examples include directed partially ordered sets. A functor indexed by a filtered category is called filtered, and its colimit is a filtered direct limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modules as filtered colimits of finitely generated submodules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every module M is the filtered direct limit of its finitely generated submodules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (7.3). This provides a standard way to write arbitrary modules as colimits of 'finite' pieces; used later in Lazard's theorem for flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct sums as filtered colimits of finite subsums
rubrics_metrics.description: Every direct sum of modules is the filtered direct limit of its finite direct subsums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (7.4). Useful to reduce statements about arbitrary sums to finite ones via filtered colimits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete construction of filtered colimit (sets/modules/algebras)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a functor M_i indexed by a filtered category I, the colimit M is the disjoint union ⨄ M_i modulo the equivalence relation: m_i ~ m_j iff there exists a transition map to some k making their images equal. Insertions are given by canonical maps M_i -> M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition (7.7). Proof verifies reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity using filteredness, then defines addition and scalar multiplication for modules and verifies well-definedness. Also describes universal property and how maps out of colimit are induced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifting properties in filtered colimits
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Every element of lim M_i comes from some stage M_i. (2) Equalities between inserted elements are witnessed at some later stage. (3) If an inserted element maps to zero in the colimit, it becomes zero at some later stage (for modules/algebras).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary (7.8). These practical properties are frequently used to reduce statements about the colimit to statements about some index stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtered direct limits are exact (preserve exactness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filtered direct limits are exact functors on the category of 3-term exact sequences of R-modules: applying lim_I to a diagram of exact sequences indexed by a filtered category yields an exact sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (7.10). Proof uses lifting properties (7.8) to show Im = Ker after taking colimit. This is a key homological property: filtered colimits commute with taking kernels/cokernels appropriately to preserve exactness of short sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hom commutes with filtered colimits for finitely presented inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The canonical map lim Hom(N, M_i) -> Hom(N, lim M_i) is injective if N is finitely generated, and bijective if N is finitely presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition (7.12). Proof reduces to free/presented modules and uses exactness of filtered colimits (7.10) together with Hom preserving finite direct sums. Use presentation of N and diagram chase to get injectivity/surjectivity criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal mapping property (UMP) of tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: For modules M,N over R, the canonical bilinear map τ : M × N -> M ⊗_R N is universal: Hom_R(M⊗_R N, P) ≅ Bil_R(M,N;P) as R-modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (8.3). Construct M⊗N as quotient of free module on M×N by relations (8.2.1). Use UMP to identify maps out of tensor product with bilinear maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifunctoriality of tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: Given homomorphisms f : M -> M' and g : N -> N', there is an induced map f⊗g : M ⊗ N -> M' ⊗ N' making the evident diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section (8.4). The UMP gives existence/uniqueness. Consequence: M⊗- and -⊗N are linear functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutative and unit laws for tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: Switch map induces M ⊗_R N ≅ N ⊗_R M (commutativity). R ⊗_R M ≅ M via 1⊗m -> m (unit law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition (8.5). Proofs use the switch on generators and the bilinearity/UMP for the unit isomorphism. These give basic symmetries used when manipulating tensors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product with bimodules and extension of scalars
rubrics_metrics.description: If N is an (R,R')-bimodule, then M⊗_R N is an (R,R')-bimodule with R'-action x'(m⊗n)=m⊗(x'n). If R' is an R-algebra, M⊗_R R' is the extension of scalars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section (8.7). Bifunctoriality ensures the two multiplications commute; use to transport module structures across tensoring by algebras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative law and adjoint associativity of tensor
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical isomorphisms: M ⊗_R (N ⊗_{R'} P) ≅ (M ⊗_R N) ⊗_{R'} P (associativity) and Hom_{R'}(M⊗_R N, P) ≅ Hom_R(M, Hom_{R'}(N,P)) (adjoint associativity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (8.9). Proof uses universality of trilinear maps and the UMP of tensor product; adjoint associativity is essential for many hom-tensor adjunction arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensoring with an algebra is left adjoint to restriction of scalars (cancellation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R' is an R-algebra, then (M ⊗_R R') ⊗_{R'} P = M ⊗_R P and Hom_{R'}(M ⊗_R R', P) = Hom_R(M, P); equivalently, ⊗ R' is left adjoint to restriction of scalars, and Hom_{R'}(R, -) is a right adjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary (8.10). Interprets tensoring by R' as a left adjoint (extension of scalars) and Hom_{R'}(R,-) as the corresponding right adjoint (restriction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product functor preserves direct limits
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fixed bimodule N, the functor - ⊗_R N preserves direct limits (equivalently, direct sums and cokernels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary (8.11). Follows since -⊗N is a left adjoint (adjoint associativity) and left adjoints preserve colimits (6.12). Useful when exchanging colimits with tensor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensoring can fail to preserve injections/kernels
rubrics_metrics.description: Tensor product does not necessarily preserve kernels or injective maps: example Z --×2--> Z tensor Z/2 yields zero map, so an injection can become zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (8.12). This is a critical counterexample showing tensoring is only right exact in general and can kill torsion; motivates notion of flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watts characterization of linear functors
rubrics_metrics.description: For a linear functor F : R-mod -> R-mod, there is a natural map M ⊗ F(R) -> F(M) with F(R) = N, and this map is an isomorphism iff F preserves direct sums and cokernels. In other words, such F are tensor-by-a-module functors exactly when they commute with sums and cokernels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem (8.15). Proof constructs the natural transformation via Hom(R,-) and adjoint associativity; preservation of sums/cokernels is checked via presentations and diagram chase. Use to identify representable/tensor functors among linear functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive functors preserve finite direct sums and are Z-linear
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor that preserves finite direct sums is additive (Z-linear). Conversely, additive functors preserve finite direct sums; but additivity alone may not imply R-linearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections (8.16) and (8.17). Example given: complex conjugation on C-vector spaces is additive but not C-linear. Use to separate notions of additivity vs R-linearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equational criterion for vanishing in a tensor product
rubrics_metrics.description: Given generators n_j of N, an element ∑ m_i ⊗ n_i = 0 in M⊗N iff there exist finitely many m_k' ∈ M and scalars x_{i,k} ∈ R with m_i = ∑_k x_{i,k} m_k' for all i and ∑_i x_{i,k} n_i = 0 for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma (8.18). Provides an explicit finite 'matrix' witness for vanishing of a tensor; proof uses a presentation of N and exactness (8.11). Useful computationally to detect zero tensors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product of algebras is coproduct in R-alg
rubrics_metrics.description: For R-algebras S and T, the tensor product S ⊗_R T with canonical maps s ↦ s⊗1 and t ↦ 1⊗t is an R-algebra which is the coproduct of S and T in the category of R-algebras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section (8.19). The universal property is shown by bijection between Hom_{R-alg}(S⊗ T, V) and pairs of algebra maps (S→V, T→V) commuting with R-structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of exactness, left exactness, right exactness for functors
rubrics_metrics.description: An R-linear functor F is exact if it preserves exact sequences; left exact if it preserves kernels; right exact if it preserves cokernels. Examples: Hom(P,-) is exact iff P is projective; Hom(N,-) (contravariant) is left exact; M⊗- is right exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section (9.2). These definitions set stage for flatness: a module is flat iff tensoring with it is exact. The examples connect categorical properties to module-theoretic notions (projective, flat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent formulations of exactness for linear functors
rubrics_metrics.description: For an R-linear functor F, the following are equivalent: (1) F preserves exact sequences (exact), (2) F preserves short exact sequences, (3) F preserves kernels and surjections, (4) F preserves cokernels and injections, (5) F preserves kernels and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition (9.3). These equivalences allow checking exactness via a variety of concrete properties depending on context; useful when verifying exactness in practice.
